per_question.user_input: Can I deduct points paid when I took out a mortgage to purchase my main home?
per_question.response:
Yes, you may be able to deduct points paid when you took out a mortgage to purchase your main home — and in many cases, you can **fully deduct them in the year paid**. Here's a detailed breakdown:

---

## General Rule
Points are considered prepaid interest, so they are **generally deducted ratably (spread out) over the life of the mortgage** [Pub 936, pp.7-8]. However, there is an important exception for home purchase loans.

---

## Full Deduction in the Year Paid
You can **fully deduct points in the year paid** if you meet **all** of the following tests [Pub 936, pp.7-8]:

1. Your loan is **secured by your main home** (the home you ordinarily live in most of the time).
2. Paying points is an **established business practice** in the area where the loan was made.
3. The points paid were **not more than the points generally charged** in that area.
4. You use the **cash method of accounting** (you report income when received and deduct expenses when paid — most individuals use this method).
5. The points were **not paid in place of amounts** ordinarily stated separately on the settlement statement (such as appraisal fees, inspection fees, title fees, attorney fees, and property taxes).
6. The **funds you provided** at or before closing, plus any points the seller paid, were **at least as much as the points charged**. These funds can include a down payment, escrow deposit, earnest money, or other funds paid at or before closing — but you cannot have borrowed them from your lender or mortgage broker.
7. You used the loan to **buy or build your main home**.
8. The points were **figured as a percentage** of the principal amount of the mortgage.
9. The amount is **clearly shown on the settlement statement** (such as Form HUD-1) as points charged for the mortgage.

> **If you meet all of these tests, you can choose to either fully deduct the points in the year paid, or deduct them over the life of the loan** [Pub 936, p.8].

---

## What If You Don't Fully Meet the Tests?

- **Funds provided were less than points charged (Test 6 not fully met):** You can still deduct points in the year paid, but only **up to the amount of funds you provided**. The remainder is spread over the life of the loan. For example, if you were charged $1,000 in points but only provided a $750 down payment, you can deduct $750 in the year paid and spread the remaining $250 over the life of the mortgage [Pub 936, p.9].

- **Seller-paid points:** A borrower is treated as paying any points that the home seller pays on the borrower's behalf. These can count toward your deduction as well [Pub 936, pp.7-8].

- **Points exceed what's generally charged (Test 3 not fully met):** You can deduct only the points generally charged in your area in the year paid. Any excess must be spread over the life of the mortgage [Pub 936, p.9].

---

## Important Distinctions
- Points on a **second home** cannot be fully deducted in the year paid — they must be deducted only over the life of the loan [Pub 936, p.8].
- Points paid to **refinance** a mortgage are generally **not** fully deductible in the year paid, even if the new mortgage is secured by your main home [Pub 936, p.8].

---

**In summary:** If your points were paid to purchase your main home and you meet all nine tests listed above, you can fully deduct those points in the year you paid them on Schedule A (Form 1040) [Pub 936, pp.7-8].

per_question.user_input: Can I deduct interest on a home equity loan used to pay off credit card debt?
per_question.response:
**No, you generally cannot deduct interest on a home equity loan used to pay off credit card debt.**

The IRS is very clear on this point: interest on home equity loans and lines of credit is deductible **only if the borrowed funds are used to buy, build, or substantially improve the taxpayer's home that secures the loan** [Pub 936, p.2]. Using the loan proceeds to pay off credit card debt does **not** qualify for this deduction, as that is a personal expense, not a home improvement.

This rule is reinforced when it comes to reporting: any interest shown on Form 1098 from a home equity loan "is **not deductible** if the proceeds were not used to buy, build, or substantially improve a qualified home" [Pub 936, p.10].

Additionally, the loan must be secured by your main home or second home (a "qualified residence") and meet other requirements [Pub 936, p.2]. Even if your home equity loan is secured by your home, the **use of the funds** is the determining factor — and paying off credit card debt fails that test.

**In summary:** If you took out a home equity loan to pay off credit card debt, the interest you paid on that loan is **not deductible** as home mortgage interest.

per_question.user_input: What is the maximum American Opportunity Tax Credit per eligible student?
per_question.response:
The maximum American Opportunity Tax Credit is **$2,500 per eligible student** for 2025 [p970, pp.9-10].

Here's how the credit is calculated [p970, p.19]:
1. **100%** of the first **$2,000** of qualified education expenses paid for the eligible student, **plus**
2. **25%** of the next **$2,000** of qualified education expenses paid for that student.

To claim the full $2,500, you must have paid at least **$4,000** of adjusted qualified education expenses for the eligible student [p970, p.19].

Additionally, **40% of the credit (up to $1,000) may be refundable**, while the remaining 60% is nonrefundable [p970, pp.9-10].

Note that the credit may be reduced or eliminated based on your Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) — the phase-out begins at **$160,000 for married filing jointly** and **$80,000 for single filers** (with full phase-out at $180,000 and $90,000, respectively) [p970, pp.9-10].

per_question.user_input: What is the modified AGI phase-out range for the American Opportunity Tax Credit for single filers?
per_question.response:
For single filers (as well as head of household and qualifying surviving spouse filers), the modified AGI phase-out range for the American Opportunity Tax Credit is **$80,000 to $90,000** [p970, p.20].

Specifically:
- The credit begins to phase out when MAGI exceeds **$80,000** [p970, p.20].
- The credit is **completely eliminated** when MAGI reaches **$90,000 or more** [p970, p.20].
- The MAGI limit is confirmed in the overview table as **$90,000 if single, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse** [p970, p.10].

This means the phase-out range spans **$10,000** ($80,000–$90,000) for single filers, compared to $160,000–$180,000 for those filing a joint return [p970, p.20].

per_question.user_input: How much student loan interest can I deduct per year?
per_question.response:
The maximum student loan interest deduction is generally **$2,500 per year** (or the actual interest you paid during the tax year, if less) [p970, p.33]. Here are the key details:

---

### Maximum Deduction
Your student loan interest deduction is the **smaller of**:
- **$2,500**, or
- The interest you actually paid during the tax year [p970, pp.33-34].

---

### Income Phase-Out (for 2025)
The deduction may be **gradually reduced or eliminated** based on your Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) [p970, p.30]:

| Filing Status | Phase-Out Begins | Fully Eliminated At |
|---|---|---|
| Single / Other | $85,000 | $100,000 |
| Married Filing Jointly | $170,000 | $200,000 |

For example, if you are married filing jointly with a MAGI of $185,000 and paid $2,750 in interest, your maximum deduction of $2,500 would be reduced by $1,250 (calculated as $2,500 × ($185,000 − $170,000) / $30,000), leaving you with a reduced deduction of **$1,250** [p970, p.35].

---

### Eligibility Requirements
You can claim the deduction if **all** of the following are met [p970, p.33]:
- Your filing status is **not** married filing separately.
- No one else is claiming you as a dependent.
- You are **legally obligated** to pay interest on a qualified student loan.
- You actually **paid interest** on a qualified student loan.

---

### How to Claim It
This is an **adjustment to income**, meaning you can claim it even if you don't itemize deductions. Enter the allowable amount on **Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 21** [p970, pp.35-36].

---

### What Cannot Be Deducted
You **cannot** deduct the following as student loan interest [p970, p.33]:
- Interest you are not legally obligated to pay.
- Certain loan origination fees (payments for property or services by the lender).
- Interest paid through the National Health Service Corps Loan Repayment Program or similar programs.
- Interest paid by your employer after March 27, 2020, under an educational assistance program.

per_question.user_input: What is the Lifetime Learning Credit and how does it differ from the American Opportunity Credit?
per_question.response:
## The Lifetime Learning Credit and How It Differs from the American Opportunity Credit

### What is the Lifetime Learning Credit?

The **Lifetime Learning Credit** is one of two tax credits available for 2025 to help offset the costs of higher education by reducing the amount of income tax you owe [p970, pp.21-22]. For the tax year, you may be able to claim a lifetime learning credit of **up to $2,000** for qualified education expenses paid for all eligible students [p970, pp.22-23].

Unlike a deduction (which reduces the amount of income subject to tax), a tax credit directly reduces the tax itself. However, the Lifetime Learning Credit is a **nonrefundable credit**, meaning it can reduce your tax to zero, but if the credit is more than your tax, the excess will **not** be refunded to you [p970, p.22].

Your allowable credit may also be limited by your income. For 2025, the credit is gradually phased out if your **Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI)** is between **$80,000 and $90,000** (or between **$160,000 and $180,000** if you file a joint return) [p970, p.21].

---

### Key Differences Between the Lifetime Learning Credit and the American Opportunity Credit

| Feature | Lifetime Learning Credit | American Opportunity Credit |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum credit** | Up to $2,000 for all eligible students | Up to $2,500 per eligible student [p970, p.9] |
| **Year limit** | **No limit** on the number of years it can be claimed per student [p970, pp.22-23] | Limited to **no more than 4 tax years** per student [p970, pp.22-23] |
| **Eligible student definition** | A student enrolled in **one or more courses** at an eligible educational institution [p970, pp.75-76] | Must be enrolled **at least half-time** in a degree/credential program, must not have completed the first 4 years of postsecondary education, and must have no federal or state felony drug conviction [p970, pp.75-76] |
| **Refundability** | **Nonrefundable** only [p970, p.22] | Has both a refundable and nonrefundable portion [p970, p.21] |
| **Credit amount comparison** | Generally lower | If you have the choice, the American Opportunity Credit will **always be greater** than the Lifetime Learning Credit [p970, p.22] |

---

### Can You Claim Both Credits?

**No.** For each student, you can elect only one of the credits for any given year. For example, if you claim the Lifetime Learning Credit for a child on your 2025 return, you cannot also claim the American Opportunity Credit for that same child in 2025 [p970, p.22].

However, if you pay qualified education expenses for **more than one student** in the same year, you can claim the American Opportunity Credit for one student and the Lifetime Learning Credit for another student in the same year [p970, pp.21-22].

per_question.user_input: Are prizes and contest winnings taxable income?
per_question.response:
Yes, prizes and contest winnings are generally taxable income. Here is a detailed breakdown:

## General Rule
If you win a prize in a lucky number drawing, television or radio quiz program, beauty contest, or other event, you must include it in your income. For example, if you win a $50 prize in a photography contest, you must report this income on **Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8i** [p525, p.35]. Prizes and awards in goods or services must also be included in your income at their **fair market value (FMV)** [p17, pp.77-78].

## Refusing a Prize
If you **refuse to accept a prize**, you do not have to include its value in your income [p525, p.35].

## Employee Awards or Bonuses
Cash awards or bonuses given to you by your employer for good work or suggestions must generally be included in your income as **wages**. However, certain noncash employee achievement awards can be excluded from income [p525, p.35].

## Prize Points
If you're a salesperson and receive prize points redeemable for merchandise awarded by a distributor or manufacturer, you must include their FMV in your income. These prize points are taxable in the year they're **paid or made available to you**, rather than in the year you redeem them for merchandise [p525, p.35].

## Pulitzer, Nobel, and Similar Prizes
If you were awarded a prize in recognition of accomplishments in religious, charitable, scientific, artistic, educational, literary, or civic fields, you must generally include the value of the prize in your income. However, you may **exclude** this prize from income if you meet **all** of the following requirements [p525, p.35]:
1. You were selected **without any action on your part** to enter the contest or proceeding.
2. You are **not required to perform substantial future services** as a condition for receiving the prize or award.
3. The prize or award is **transferred by the payer directly to a governmental unit or tax-exempt charitable organization** as designated by you — and you cannot use the prize before it is transferred [p525, p.35].

## Scholarship Prizes
Scholarship prizes won in a contest are **not** considered scholarships or fellowships if you don't have to use the prizes for educational purposes. You must include these amounts in your income on **Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8i**, whether or not you use the amounts for educational purposes [p525, p.36].

## Gambling Winnings, Lotteries, and Raffles
Gambling winnings — including winnings from fantasy sports leagues, lotteries, and raffles — must be included in your income on **Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8b**. In addition to cash winnings, you must include in your income the FMV of bonds, cars, houses, and other noncash prizes. If you itemize deductions, you can deduct gambling losses, but only up to the amount of your winnings [p17, pp.77-78].
